Evaluating the Influence of Mulsemedia Content in Reading
Natália Vieira, Anderson Pinto, Felipe Silva, Helder Okuno, Iury Amorim, Taymison Ramos,
Diego Haddad, Glauco Amorim, Gustavo Paiva Guedes, Joel dos Santos
CEFET/RJ

(diego.haddad,glauco.amorim,gustavo.guedes,joel.santos)@cefet-rj.br
ABSTRACT
Augmented e-books provide the reader with a better quality of
experience (QoE) by enriching the e-books with multimedia content
and interactive elements. In the multimedia field, an improve in
QoE has been performed by the use of sensory effects, creating the
so-called mulsemedia applications. In this paper, it is considered

In this paper, it is considered
that e-books augmented with mulsemedia content influence the
reader perception of the history environment, besides improving its
QoE. It is presented a mulsemedia setup with light, wind and audio
effects, which are synchronizedwith a written history. Among other
discoveries, the collected data suggest that such elements have a
more significant influence on the reader when the environment
description tend to be vague, whereas in scenes whose details are
precisely described this influence is rather minored.

• Software and its engineering→ Virtual worlds software;

1 INTRODUCTION
Reading is a learning process whose importance is evidenced from
the early years until the most advanced ones [6, 14]. The early
mastering of the decoding process demanded by reading is known
to help to promote personal development through a person’s life
(in education, career or even for reaching predefined goals) [6].

Even in advanced ages, mastering the reading process may increase

self-esteem and helps to satisfy the human being innate curiosity
[14].
Nowadays, electronic books (e-books) reading is increasing in
popularity [4]. E-books present several benefits when compared to
paper books. For example, readers from different places in the world
do not need to wait for the impression and distribution of a book,
since they can buy its electronic version as soon as it is available [10].
Furthermore, e-books are more efficient than paper books regarding
storage, transfer and accessibility [8]. Moreover, e-books may be
enrichedwithmultimedia content (e.g., audio, video) and interactive
elements (e.g., hyperlinks), promoting a better quality of experience
(QoE) to its users [3, 13].

In multimedia, works such as [12, 15] present an increase in QoE
by the inclusion of sensory effects in applications. Applications
where traditional multimedia content is synchronized with sensory
effects have been called MulSeMedia (multissensorial media) [5].
In this work, e-books enriched with mulsemedia content are called
multissensorial electronic books or, for simplicity, multissensorial
books [7].
Besides promoting a better QoE, studies indicate multissensorial
books may engage children in reading [2]. Also, they may improve
the teaching/learning process [13]. Thus, some works [1, 9] evalu-
ated through experiments the beneficial influence of mulsemedia
content in learning.
In this context, the present work aims at evaluating the influence

In this context, the present work aims at evaluating the influence
of adding mulsemedia elements in reading, as well as its impact
on the reader’s experience. An experiment was conducted with 14
participants, where audio elements, wind and light effects were
synchronized with a story reading. At the end of the experiment,
readers answered an evaluation questionnaire. Experiments indi-
cate an impact in the interpretation of the ambient described in the
text, given the addition of such content.
The remaining of this paper is structured as follows. Section 2
presents related work. Section 3 discusses the experiment, pre-
senting how it was conducted and the prototype used. Section 4
discusses the experiment results. At last, Section 5 concludes the
paper and present future work.

At last, Section 5 concludes the
paper and present future work.
2 RELATEDWORK
This section presents related work published in the literature that
aims at enriching e-books with the objective of influencing the
learning quality [1, 9, 11].
In [11], the authors propose an e-book capable of presenting
images and producing vibration effects synchronized with a textual
content. Vibration effects are delivered through a jacket and a sofa.
Images are presented using a second screen connected to the e-book.
The experiments indicated an improvement in QoE, although it was
133

not possible to determine the importance of the haptic experience
in learning. An extension of this work is presented in [1], where

An extension of this work is presented in [1], where
the authors included a haptic wristband, an audio system, and a TV.
The authors conducted five experiments. Their results indicated
a considerable improvement in the readers’ experience, either in
learning or entertainment. In [9], the authors proposed the use of
physical agents to enrich a textual content and provide a deeper
learning experience. Thework presented as a physical agent, a robot
that interacts with the reader. Although the authors emphasize
that their proposal helps the text comprehension, no quantitative
evaluation was presented.
Different from the works presented in [1, 9, 11], this paper con-
ducts an experiment to evaluate the impact of the inclusion of
mulsemedia content in the reading process. In [1, 11] the haptic

In [1, 11] the haptic
effect generation depends on human interaction. Thus, the reader
has to touch the reading device so that a haptic effect is delivered.
In the experiment conducted in this paper, mulsemedia content
is presented automatically as the reading unfolds. A limitation of
the prototype presented here concerns the granularity with which
mulsemedia content is synchronized with the reading. Currently, it
allows only the synchronization with each paragraph of the text. It
is worth noticing, however, that such limitation is also present in
[1, 11].
3 EXPERIMENT
The experiments aimed at evaluating the impact of the inclusion of
mulsemedia content in the reader’s perception regarding a story
reading. A multissensorial book prototype was developed for con-

A multissensorial book prototype was developed for con-
ducting the experiments. It is capable of synchronizing audio con-
tent and sensory effects with the reading content. The following
sections present the prototype architechture (Section 3.1), the story
used in the experiments (Section 3.2) and how the experiments
were conducted (Section 3.3).
3.1 Prototype Architechture
The multissensorial book prototype was developed according to
the architecture presented in Figure 1. The reader component is
responsible for the user interface, presenting to her excerpts of
the story. As the reading unfolds, events regarding the change of
excerpts are sent to the effects server component, which acts as the
interface with actuators present in the physical ambient.

Figure 1: Multissensorial book prototype architecture used
in the experiments. The prototype is composed of two main
components: the reader and the effects server.
The reader component was developed in HTML. Its interface
is composed of a text paragraph and a button. Once pressed, the
button triggers a function that repaints the screen with the next
paragraph to be read and sends one or more events to the server.
The text to be presented and the annotation about the sensory
effects to be executed are stored in a json file in the server. This
file has a list of objects with the fields paragraph and params. Each
paragraph object stores a text paragraph and each params object

Each
paragraph object stores a text paragraph and each params object
stores a list of events to be sent when that paragraph starts to be
read. At the moment the reader component and the server establish
a connection (through a GET request to the root URL) that infor-
mation is transformed into an HTML file that is sent to the reader
component. Events are sent through POST requests to the suffix
/action, with the events as parameters. Furthermore, it is possible
to specify a delay for the execution of a given effect, whenever such
precision is necessary.
Figure 2: Prototype configuration in two activation mo-

The effects server component was developed in Python and exe-

The effects server component was developed in Python and exe-
cuted in a Raspberry Pi. The server development used (i) the Flask
framework for constructing the REST API used to communicate
with the reader, (ii) the mixer module of library pygame for audio
execution, and (iii) the GPIO module of library RPi for the commu-
nication with actuators. The prototype has as actuators two white
led lamps (L1 and L2), one color lamp (L3), one headset/speaker (S),
and four fans activated together (V ). The white lamps have different
power, thus allowing when used together four illumination levels
(high, medium, low and dark). Figure 2 presents the prototype con-
figuration in two distinct moments: with high illumination and
with the color lamp active. In the figure, it is possible to observe

In the figure, it is possible to observe
the disposition of the different actuators. It is worth noting that a
smartphone was used for the reader component in the experiments.
3.2 Story
For the experiments, a medieval action story was created, inspired
in an RPG game. This choicewas based on the adequacy of such kind
of story for the use of sensory effects, given that it describes several
situations that can be observed through sounds, illumination, and
wind. Throughout the story, sensory effects are used to compose
the ambient described in the text. The story development, as well

as the inclusion of sensory effects, followed the following criteria:
(i) most of the effects should be concentrated in the second half of
the story, giving the user time to immerse in the story before the
effects begin to be executed; (ii) not all paragraph should have an
effect so that the expectation is maintained; (iii) the audio effects
should represent ambient sounds and onomatopoeias relative to
some action performed by the characters; (iv) all the effects (sound,
wind, and light) used in the representation of the story ambient
should have a counterpart in the text, i.e., if a wind effect is executed

in some point, such phenomenon should be described in the text.
Regarding the light effects, the four illumination levels (high,
medium, low and dark) were used for indicating the ambient illu-
mination, while the color light was used for the story excerpts with
the presence of magic. Moreover, delays were used so that ambient
sounds and onomatopoeias could be executed as close as possible
to the moment it was read.
Figure 3 present a timeline indicating the effects used and the
moment they are executed throughout the story. Considering that
each reader has a reading pace, the time indicated in Figure 3 is an
approximated value. In this timeline it was considered a reading
time of approximately 15 minutes, with an average of 20 seconds

per paragraph. In the figure, the paragraph number is represented
in blue and its reading moment (in seconds) in black. Green marks
represent audio effects, the red ones represent light effects, and the
yellow ones represent wind effects.
3.3 Experiments Conduction
The experiments were conducted with 14 participants, all of them
first-semester students of Computer Science undergraduate course.
Each participant read the story separated from the others. The
experiment routine consisted of an instruction period, followed by
the story reading and, at last, the evaluation questionnaire filling.
Given the objective of evaluating the influence of mulsemedia
content in reading, test subjects were divided into two groups. One
group read the story with sensory effects (CE) and the other read

One
group read the story with sensory effects (CE) and the other read
the story without sensory effects (SE). Subjects were assigned to
each group randomly and were not informed of their group prior
to reading. During the instruction period, it was indicated to the
participant how to use the reader and to perform the reading out
loud. It was necessary so that we could follow the subject’s reading
pace and effect occurrence.
The evaluation questionnaire is composed of 8 questions, besides
a field for critics and suggestions. Each questionwas evaluated using
a Likert scale from 1 to 6. Two questions of the questionnaire focus
on measuring the subject perception about the experience and the
six other questions measure the influence of mulsemedia content.

The questions related to the user experience asked if the subject
“considered his/her reading experience intense” and if the subject
“had the sensation that several of his/her senses were stimulated
during reading”. The questions related to the subject perception
about the story ambient in different parts of the text are presented
in the following paragraphs.
Paragraphs 7 − 10: the city presented in those paragraphs is
described as active and agitated. It is executed an audio effect in
paragraph 8 of an intense chattering. The subject had to evaluate
the city mood from peace and calm (1) to tumult and agitation (6).
Paragraphs 14 − 16: a fight takes place and audio effects of a
sword battle and agony sounds are executed. The subject had to

The subject had to
evaluate the fight from without consequences (1) to bloody (6).
Paragraphs 18 − 26: the bar presented in those paragraphs
is described as a place of chattering and fights. It is used a low
illumination and sounds of chattering and breaking glasses. The
subject had to evaluate the bar ambient from very silent (1) to very
noisy (6).
Paragraphs 27 − 29: the characters pass by a village at the end
of the afternoon. It is used a medium illumination and sounds of
steps. The subject had to evaluate the village ambient from very
dark (1) to very lightened (6).
Paragraphs 30− 34: the forest presented in those paragraphs is
described as a lugubrious ambient. At this point, the reading ambi-
ent is kept dark, except by the reader screen light. The subject had

The subject had
to evaluate the forest ambient from very dark (1) to very lightened
(6).
Paragraphs 38 − 43: the characters fight against creatures de-
scribed as emitting low whispers. At this point, whisper audios
are used. The subject had to evaluate the sound emitted by the
creatures from inaudible (1) to very loud (6).
4 EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS
On average, subjects took 13minutes to read the story. Experiment
results are summarized in Figure 4. The graphic presents the average
and the confidence interval (for a 95% confidence level) for the
evaluations of each of the questions presented above. Blue bars
present the results for test subjects that were in the group with
sensory effects (CE) and gray bars present the results for the ones
in the group without sensory effects (SE).

As can be seen in the figure, is was observed a significative differ-
ence regarding the CE group perception about how agitated was the
city (1st bar). This result is expected given the city description and
the sound effects used in this excerpt. Another difference is about
the mistaken evaluation about the sound emitted by the creatures
at the end of the story (6th bar). This difference may be explained

Regarding the perception of the fight (2nd bar) and the village
(4th bar), the evaluations point to a difference, although it has no
statistical difference. The fight seems to be perceived as less bloody
and the village as less dark by the CE group. Regarding the fight, a
possible explanation for the less bloody perception lies in the fact
that the sounds used to represent it were, in fact, no bloody. More-
over, the description in that excerpt was not precise about the fight
brutality. Regarding the village, given the ambiguous description of
“end of afternoon”, the effect of medium illumination seems to act
as the noticeable element for the ambient perception. Finally, that

Finally, that
was a slight variation between the groups in the evaluation of the
bar ambient (3rd bar) and the forest (5th bar). We believe that the
ambient description leaves less margin for the reader’s imagination,
weakening the influence of the effects on the subject’s perception
of those ambients.
The two last bars present the results for the questions about
the experience perceived by test subjects. As one can see, the CE
group evaluated the reading experience as more intense (7th bar) a
with more stimulus to its senses (8th bar) when compared to the
SE group.
5 CONCLUSION
Multissensorial books have the possibility to encourage reading
and promote a better reading/learning process. This work objective
was to evaluate the influence of mulsemedia elements inclusion in

This work objective
was to evaluate the influence of mulsemedia elements inclusion in
reading. An experiment was conducted with 14 participants, and
audio elements, wind and light effects were synchronized with the
textual content.
At the end of the experiment, test subjects had to answer a
questionnaire with objective questions. Six questions measured
the subject perception about the story ambient at different points
of the text. Experiments indicate that in two points mulsemedia
content indeed influenced the ambient perception. In the remaining
points, no statistical difference was observed. However, we believe
there is a tendency of presenting a bigger difference in the subject
perception when a vague description of the ambient is presented

in the text, than when a more precise description is provided.
As future work, we seek to improve the prototype quality, allow-
ing a smaller granularity for the synchronization and the inclusion
of other mulsemedia content. Another future work is to perform
experiments with other stories and other sensory effects.
